American Gothic. Grant Wood's 1930 painting has become the archetypal symbol of rural American character and values, depicting a farmer and his daughter standing before a Gothic Revival farmhouse, their expressions stern and suspicious.

The painting was displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it won a bronze medal at the Carnegie International and immediately became an American cultural icon. It shows a farmer holding a pitchfork and a young woman in a simple white dress standing before a farmhouse with a distinctive pointed window. Their expressions are closed and wary. The composition is rigorously frontal and austere, emphasizing social distance and emotional reserve.

Wood drew on his Iowa upbringing and his admiration for Northern European Renaissance painting, especially Flemish techniques, to create a style he called Regionalism. The work has been read as satirical commentary on rural conservatism, or as a sincere celebration of American agrarian character, an ambiguity that has fueled decades of debate. It became so iconic that it spawned countless parodies and reinterpretations, becoming a shorthand for heartland America in visual culture.
